beats.text: Kodak invented the digital camera... then buried it. Why?
beats.dir: intriguing hook, a little playful, pause before 'then buried it', rising question at the end

beats.text: It's 1975. A Kodak engineer, Steve Sasson, builds the world's first portable digital camera.
But it looks less like an iPhone, and more like a toaster that went to engineering college.
It weighs 3.6 kilograms, uses 16 batteries, and captures a shocking zero point zero one megapixels.
beats.dir: listing facts, building to amused disbelief on 'zero point zero one'

beats.text: One photo takes 23 seconds just to save to a cassette tape. Yes. A cassette tape.
beats.dir: deadpan, short pause before 'Yes. A cassette tape.'

beats.text: And when Sasson shows it to his bosses? Reportedly: That's cute. But don't tell anyone.
beats.dir: conspiratorial, lower voice on the quote

beats.text: Why hide something this revolutionary? Because Kodak made its money from film.
beats.dir: curious question, then a confident reveal

beats.text: Every photo meant film, developing and prints. A digital photo? No film. No prints. No repeat business.
beats.dir: brisk, punchy, staccato on the last three short sentences

beats.text: So Kodak protected the past, while the future quietly loaded. Then smartphones put a camera in everyone's pocket.
In 2012, Kodak filed for bankruptcy. The company that invented digital photography was disrupted by it.
beats.dir: heavy, sober, slower on the last words

beats.text: Kodak didn't fail because it couldn't see the future. It failed because it was too afraid to lose the present.
